reconnaissance_summary.censorship_and_self_censorship: Independent media and civil society operated under censorship, surveillance, intimidation, arbitrary detention, and restricted protest space; criticism remained possible through international NGOs, selected civil-society organizations, international reporting, and external institutional sources.
chapter_specific_biases: 1B is concentrated in official diplomatic, regulatory, and project records; safeguards conclusions and personal command conduct remain unresolved.
2B distinguishes conflict exposure from initiation and responsibility; Sinai reporting is constrained and official peace claims lack independent corroboration.
3B is NGO-concentrated and lacks complete command-chain, group-specific, and domestic-remedy documentation.
4B combines structured indicators, official dialogue records, and external political analysis; meaningful participation and institutional checks remain uncertain.
5B separates macroeconomic shocks, formal commitments, program reach, and household outcomes; military opacity and causal attribution remain limitations.
6B includes independent Takaful evaluation but lacks broad service-quality, affordability, regional, and political-conditionality evidence.
7B is institutional and network-level; no personal-integrity nexus was established.
8B documents policy identification and implementation caveats, but not portfolio-wide outcomes, personnel quality, or corrective adaptation.
reconnaissance_summary.complaint_volume_interpretation: Arrest, detention, incident, complaint, program-reach, and reporting counts cannot be interpreted as population prevalence without denominators. Restricted access and selective visibility may undercount harm; visible complaints may also reflect reporting access.
reconnaissance_summary.criticism_possible: Criticism was documented through Amnesty, Human Rights Watch, CIHRS, DAWN, Carnegie, IFPRI, World Bank, IAEA, EIPR, and international reporting. Domestic criticism was constrained and the evidence is not representative of all affected populations.
reconnaissance_summary.duplicate_event_risk: P001–P004 are distinct Amnesty claims from one source family; P007/P018 overlap on dialogue design; P008/P012 overlap on reform commitments; P010/P011 may repeat program claims; P021–P023 share one diplomatic statement; P025–P029 and P035–P037 overlap on El Dabaa activity; P047/P048 overlap on Takaful findings.
reconnaissance_summary.inherited_conditions_shocks_and_authorit: Sisi held formal presidential and supreme-command authority. Practical authority was constrained by military institutions, security agencies, ministries, external financing, IMF conditionality, regional conflict, the Russia–Ukraine shock, inflation, and inherited institutional capacity. Local priors generally establish country or institutional context rather than personal responsibility.
languages_and_archives_searched: English web sources and institutional archives
IMF, World Bank, IFPRI, Carnegie, U.S. government, and Egyptian official sources
reconnaissance_summary.official_statistics_reliability: Economic and military-finance figures require caution because military accounts are opaque and nominal-dollar series are not real-growth measures. Program coverage and official implementation figures are not independent welfare or quality evaluations. Conflict and casualty figures are explicitly uncertain because of Sinai security restrictions.
reconnaissance_summary.relevant_denominators: The notebook records denominators where available, including households, beneficiaries, governorates, applications, incidents, and casualties, but many repression, service-quality, civilian-harm, and political-access claims lack population denominators.
reconnaissance_summary.safe_reporting_channels: International NGOs, intergovernmental organizations, external research institutes, international media, official records, and selected civil-society organizations provided the safest documented channels. Domestic media and civil-society reporting were constrained by surveillance, intimidation, detention, and censorship.
reconnaissance_summary.source_concentration: Evidence is concentrated in Amnesty/HRW and civil-society sources for repression, official Egyptian sources for diplomatic and reform claims, IMF/World Bank/IFPRI for economic and welfare evidence, Carnegie for military-economy analysis, U.S. reporting for Sinai, and IAEA/ENRRA for nuclear matters. Independent domestic and local-language breadth remains limited.

resource_index.claim: Sisi was president throughout 2022 and Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces, supporting formal attribution for national policy, senior appointments, security policy, military operations, pardons, and major economic programs.
Amnesty reported that Sisi reactivated the Presidential Pardons Committee on 26 April 2022; releases followed recommendations, while arrests and security-agency control continued.
Released detainees were sometimes warned against activism or required to report weekly to security agencies.
Amnesty reported 766 detainee releases before COP27 but 1,540 people questioned or arrested for speech and association during the same period.

Amnesty reported that the National Human Rights Strategy was drafted without independent NGO consultation, presented a misleading rights environment, and coincided with arbitrary detention, censorship, and impunity.

Human Rights Watch and Amnesty found that authorities failed to independently investigate Ayman Hadhoud’s 2022 death in custody, concealed his death, closed the investigation, and rejected the family appeal.
Egyptian official material presented the National Dialogue, pardons, and Year of Civil Society as reform initiatives.

The 2022 terrorism report recorded at least 95 Sinai terrorist incidents and approximately 260 casualties, while noting that civilian, military, and terrorist casualty figures could not be confirmed because of security restrictions and limited reporting.

Human Rights Watch reported nearly 700 detentions across 18 governorates between 1 October and 14 November 2022, mostly under terrorism-related charges, with approximately 40 people not brought before prosecutors or of unknown whereabouts; restrictions also affected journalists, lawyers, opposition members, and activists.

CIHRS stated that the national dialogue lacked fair opposition-representation guarantees, authorities had not responded to opposition demands, and tens of thousands remained imprisoned while arrests continued; it acknowledged releases as positive but insufficient for genuine reform.

Local structured priors establish 2022 national physical-integrity, disappearance, imprisonment, killing, torture, repression, terror, and one-sided-violence context without individual orders or incitement.
